Prompt Compression Techniques

You can often say the same thing in fewer tokens. Replace verbose instructions with concise ones. Use abbreviations in internal system prompts (the model can understand them). Reference standardized formats instead of describing them. Use few-shot examples only when necessary, and when you do, keep them short and representative.

// Verbose (68 tokens)
Please analyze the following text and determine whether
the overall sentiment expressed by the author is positive,
negative, or neutral. Provide your answer as a single word.

// Concise (22 tokens)
Classify sentiment as positive/negative/neutral.
Respond with one word.

Text:

Both prompts produce equivalent results for straightforward sentiment classification, but the concise version uses 67% fewer tokens.

questions.prompt: Which strategy would have the BIGGEST impact on reducing costs for a system that processes 50,000 customer classification requests per day?

choices.text: Switching from a top-tier model to a smaller model that still handles classification accurately
Adding more examples to the prompt for better quality
Increasing the temperature for more creative classifications
Removing the system prompt entirely

questions.explanation: Classification is typically a task where smaller, cheaper models perform nearly as well as top-tier models. Switching from a model that costs $15 per million tokens to one that costs $0.25 per million tokens could reduce costs by over 98% while maintaining classification accuracy.

questions.prompt: Why are output tokens typically more expensive than input tokens?

choices.text: Output tokens contain more information
Generating output tokens requires more computation than processing input tokens
Output tokens are stored in a separate database
There is no difference in pricing between input and output tokens

questions.explanation: Generating each output token requires the full forward pass of the model, including sampling and prediction. Input tokens can be processed in parallel more efficiently. This computational asymmetry is reflected in the pricing difference.

questions.prompt: Rewrite this verbose prompt to be more token-efficient while maintaining the same functionality: 'I would like you to please carefully read through the text that I am going to provide below and then extract the person's full name, their email address, and their phone number from the text. Please format your response as a JSON object with the keys name, email, and phone.'
questions.explanation: A concise version would be something like: 'Extract from the text below and return JSON: {"name": "", "email": "", "phone": ""}. Text:' This preserves all the functional requirements (extract name/email/phone, return as JSON with specific keys) while eliminating filler words and reducing token count by roughly 60-70%.

lessons.title: Building Prompt Libraries for Teams
lessons.description: Learn how to organize, document, version, and govern a shared prompt library that scales across teams and projects.
lessons.content:
Scaling Prompt Engineering Across an Organization

As AI adoption grows within an organization, ad-hoc prompt creation by individual team members leads to inconsistent quality, duplicated effort, and a lack of institutional knowledge. A shared prompt library addresses these problems by centralizing proven prompts, establishing quality standards, and enabling collaboration.

Organizing a Prompt Library

Structure your library so that team members can quickly find what they need. A well-organized library typically categorizes prompts by function (classification, extraction, generation, analysis), by domain (customer support, marketing, engineering, legal), and by complexity level (simple, intermediate, advanced).

prompts/
  classification/
    sentiment-analysis.yaml
    ticket-routing.yaml
    content-moderation.yaml
  extraction/
    invoice-parser.yaml
    resume-parser.yaml
    meeting-action-items.yaml
  generation/
    email-drafts.yaml
    product-descriptions.yaml
    code-documentation.yaml
  analysis/
    financial-report.yaml
    competitive-analysis.yaml
    user-feedback-synthesis.yaml

Prompt Documentation Standards

Each prompt in the library should be a self-contained document that includes everything someone needs to use it effectively. A standard template might include:

  • Name and description: What the prompt does and when to use it.
  • Version: Current version number and changelog.
  • Author and reviewers: Who created and approved the prompt.
  • Variables: Required and optional parameters with descriptions and example values.
  • Model recommendation: Which model and parameters work best.
  • Test suite: A link to or inclusion of the test cases for this prompt.
  • Performance metrics: Accuracy scores, cost per call, and latency benchmarks.
  • Known limitations: Documented edge cases, failure modes, and workarounds.

Version Control and Review Process

Store prompts in version control (Git) alongside your code. Use pull requests for changes so they can be reviewed. Require that all prompt changes include updated test results showing the impact on the test suite. Maintain a changelog that records what changed, why, and what the measured impact was. This creates an audit trail and makes it easy to roll back if a change causes regressions.

Governance and Access Control

As your library grows, establish governance policies. Decide who can create new prompts, who can modify existing ones, and what review process is required. For prompts that affect customer-facing systems, you may want stricter review requirements. Consider creating a "prompt engineering guild" or center of excellence that sets standards, reviews high-impact prompts, and provides training. Document best practices in a style guide that covers naming conventions, formatting standards, testing requirements, and documentation expectations.

questions.prompt: What is the MAIN problem that a shared prompt library solves?

choices.text: It makes the AI model smarter
It eliminates inconsistent quality, duplicated effort, and loss of institutional knowledge caused by ad-hoc prompt creation
It reduces the number of API calls needed
It replaces the need for prompt engineering skills

questions.explanation: Without a shared library, teams end up independently creating similar prompts of varying quality, duplicating work, and losing the knowledge gained from testing and refining prompts. A library centralizes proven prompts and ensures consistent quality across the organization.

questions.prompt: Why should prompts be stored in version control (Git) alongside code?

choices.text: Because prompts are actually code
To enable change tracking, pull request reviews, rollbacks, and an audit trail of how prompts evolve
Because Git is the only way to store text files
To make the prompts run faster

questions.explanation: Version control gives you a complete history of every prompt change, enables peer review through pull requests, allows you to roll back to previous versions if changes cause regressions, and creates an audit trail that documents the evolution of each prompt.

questions.prompt: List at least 5 pieces of information that should be documented for every prompt in a shared team library.
questions.explanation: A complete prompt document should include: (1) Name and description of what the prompt does, (2) Version number and changelog, (3) Author and reviewers, (4) Required and optional variables with descriptions, (5) Recommended model and parameter settings, (6) Test suite or test cases, (7) Performance metrics (accuracy, cost, latency), and (8) Known limitations and edge cases. Any five of these would be a strong answer.
